stanzas.quote:
i.‘But now they only laugh with their teeth,
While their ice-block –cold eyes…’

qna.q: a) Who are ‘they’?
qna.a: They are people of modern days.

qna.q: b) Explain: ice-block-cold eyes.
qna.a: The expression ‘ice-block-cold eyes’ refers to eyes without any warmth of feeling.

qna.q: c) Identify the figure of speech used here.
qna.a: Metaphor

stanzas.quote:
ii. ‘Most of all, I want to relearn
How to laugh, for my life in the mirror
Shows only my teeth like a snake’s bare fangs!’

qna.q: a) 	Why does the poet want to relearn how to laugh?
qna.a: The poet wants to show his real feelings. Hence he wants to relearn how to laugh.

qna.q: b) Whom does the poet want to relearn from?
qna.a: The poet wants to relearn from his son.

qna.q: c) Mention the figure of speech used here.
qna.a: like a snake’s bare fangs – Simile

qna.q: a) 	With all my heart I do admire
qna.a: Athletes who sweat for fun or hire

qna.q: 1. 	Whom does the poet admire?
qna.a: The poet admires athletes.

qna.q: 2. 	For what reason do the athletes sweat?
qna.a: The athletes sweat for money or for pleasure.

qna.q: b) 	Well, ego it might be pleased enough
qna.a: But zealous athletes play so rough…..

qna.q: 1. 	What pleases the ego?
qna.a: Taking the place of a winning athlete pleases the ego.

qna.q: 2. 	Why are the athletes often rough during play?
qna.a: The athletes are often rough during play because everyone wants to win.

qna.q: c) 	When officialdom demands
qna.a: Is there a doctor in the stands?

qna.q: 1. 	Why are doctors called from stands by the sponsors?
qna.a: Whenever an athlete is injured, a doctor is sent for by the officials.

qna.q: 2. 	Why does the poet make such an observation?
qna.a: The poet is moved by the injuries of the athletes. But the umpires and referees don’t have such an emotional feeling.

qna.q: d) 	When snaps the knee and cracks the wrist……
qna.a: Identify and explain the use of the literary device in this line. Onomatopoeia 	is the literary device used in this line. 	When the athletes run for the medal they get injured. 	The sounds which come out of their parts of the body such as ‘snaps’ and ‘cracks’ are mentioned here.

title: Poem – 2 CONFESSIONS OF A BORN SPECTATOR
Poem – 3 	Lines Written in Early Spring

stanzas.quote:
(i) And ‘tis my faith that every flower
Enjoys the air it breathes…

qna.q: a) 	What is the poet’s faith?
qna.a: The poet’s faith is that the beautiful flowers enjoy every ounce of the air they breathe.

qna.q: b) What trait of Nature do we see here?
qna.a: We see the beautiful work of nature through this poem.

stanzas.quote:
(ii) And I must think, do all I can,
That there was pleasure there…

qna.q: a) 	What did the poet notice about the twigs?
qna.a: The poet noticed that the twigs expand to catch the breezy air.

qna.q: b) What was the poet’s thought about them?
qna.a: The poet thinks that the twigs or the new born branches enjoy the breeze and there is pleasure hidden there.

stanzas.quote:
(iii) If this belief from heaven be sent,
If such be Nature’s holy plan.

qna.q: a) 	What does ‘heaven’ refer to?
qna.a: Heaven refers to the place of God.

qna.q: b) Why does the poet call it ‘holy’?
qna.a: Nature is God’s work from heaven. So the poet calls it ‘holy’. stanzas.quote: i. Macavity’s a Mystery Cat: he’s called the Hidden Paw

qna.q: a) 	Does the-poet talk about a real cat?
qna.a: No, the poet talks about the fictional or imaginary cat.

qna.q: b) Why is he called the Hidden Paw?
qna.a: He is the master criminal. But he always escapes. The Scotland yard, cannot catch him. Hence he is called Hidden Paw.

stanzas.quote:
ii. He’s the bafflement of Scotland Yard, the Flying Squad’s despair: For when they reach the
scene of crime –Macavity’s not there!

qna.q: a) 	What is ‘Scotland Yard'?
qna.a: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London Metropolitan Police Service.

qna.q: b) Why does the flying squad feel disappointed?
qna.a: The flying squad rushes to the spot of crime every time to seize Macavity but he could not be found there. Hence the flying squad feels disappointed.

stanzas.quote:
iii. He sways his head from side to side, with movements like a snake;
And when you think he’s half asleep, he’s always wide awake...

qna.q: a) 	Explain the comparison made here.
qna.a: The movements of the head of the Macavity is compared to those of the snake. Macavity sways his head from side to side like a snake.

qna.q: b) What does he pretend to do?
qna.a: He pretends as if he were half asleep.

stanzas.quote: iv. For he’s a fiend in feline shape, a monster of depravity.

qna.q: a) 	How is the cat described in this lines?
qna.a: The cat is described like a devil in the shape of a cat. He is also described as the monster of depravity.

qna.q: b) Explain the phrase monster of depravity.
qna.a: It means the giant of moral corruption.

stanzas.quote: v. And his footprints are not found in any file of Scotland Yard’s.

qna.q: a) 	What seems to be a challenge for the Scotland Yard?
qna.a: Macavity never gives any clue such as his footprints in the crime spot. Since there is no trace of evidence, it seems to be a challenge for the Scotland Yard to arrest him.

qna.q: b) Why do they need his footprints?
qna.a: They need his footprints in order to arrest Macavity.

stanzas.quote: vi. It must have been Macavity!but he’s a mile away.

qna.q: a) 	What is Macavity blamed for?
qna.a: Macavityis blamed for the missing of a file of Treaty from the foreign office or the loss of some plans and drawings of Admiralty.

qna.q: b) Where is he?
qna.a: He is a mile away from the crime spot.

stanzas.quote: vii. There never was a Cat of such deceitfulness and suavity.

qna.q: a) 	Which cat is being talked of here?
qna.a: Macavity, the mysterious cat, is being talked of here.

qna.q: b) How is he different from the rest?
qna.a: He is different from the rest by the qualities such as depravity, looting, and stifling. rifling, deceitfulness and suavity.

qna.q: 1. 	Our nature it is that whatever we try
qna.a: We do with devotion deep and true

title: Poem – 5 EVEREST IS NOT THE ONLY PEAK

stanzas.quote:
i. 	Who does ‘we’ refer to?
“We” refers to all people who shoulder responsibilities.

ii. 	How should we carry out our duties?
We should carry out our duties with deep and true devotion. That is, we must be sincere in our work.

qna.q: 2. 	Defeat we repel, courage our fort

stanzas.quote:
i. 	How do we react to our defeat?
We repel defeat that we hate.We drive away defeat.

ii. 	Which is considered as our strong hold?
“Fort” means strong hold, strong point. “Courage” is our fort, our strong hold.

qna.q: 3. 	We are proud of the position, we
qna.a: Hold humble as we are

stanzas.quote:
i. 	What is the speaker proud of ?
The speaker is proud of their position

ii. 	How is the speaker both humble and proud?
The position of the speaker may be humble. But he is proud of the position.

iii. Pick out the alliteration in these lines.
Proud-position; hold – humble are the words in alliteration.

qna.q: 4. 	He, who does not stoop, is a king we adore
qna.a: We bow before competence and merit

stanzas.quote:
i. 	Who is adored as a king?
A person who does not stoop, who does not surrender is adored as a king.

ii. 	What is the figure of speech used in this line?
Metaphor

qna.q: 5. 	Honour is the property, common to all
qna.a: In dignity and pride, no need to be poor.

stanzas.quote:
i. 	Who are considered rich?
Persons who have honour, dignity and pride are considered rich.

ii. 	What is their asset?
Honour is their asset.
i) And yet ….. ground?

qna.q: a) What is the only thing we bequeath to our descendants?
qna.a: We bequeath only our deposed bodies to our descendants.

qna.q: b) What does ‘deposed’ mean?
qna.a: Deposed means removed from office or power.

qna.q: c) Are all deposed kings slain by the deposer?
qna.a: No. not all of the deposed kings are slain by the deposers, only a few. ii) And nothing…. earth

qna.q: a) What are the vanquished men left with?
qna.a: They are left with nothing.

qna.q: b) What does the ‘small model’ refer to here?
qna.a: The “small model” refers to the human body. iii) That rounds …. pomp

qna.q: a) What mocks the ruler’s power and pomp?
qna.a: Death mocks the king’s power and pomp.

qna.q: b) What hides within the crown and laughs at the grandeur?
qna.a: Death hides within the crown and laughs at the grandeur of the king. iv) Let’s talk…. epitaphs

qna.q: a) What do the three words, ‘graves, worms and epitaphs’ refer to?
qna.a: The words “graves, worms and epitaphs”-refer to our death. v) Our lands …. Bolingbroke’s

qna.q: a) Who is Bolingbroke? Is he friend or foe?
qna.a: Bolingbroke is King Richard’s cousin, but due to political reasons he becomes an enemy to King Richard. vi) To monarchize ……. looks

qna.q: a) What does a monarch’s crown symbolize?
qna.a: A monarch’s crown symbolizes the King’s power and authority over the whole country.

qna.q: b) What does the crown of rulers stand for?
qna.a: The crown of the ruler stands for the ruler’s high power and authority over the whole country. But here Shakespeare says death sits within the hollow crown. vii) As if this flesh ….our life

qna.q: a) What does ‘flesh’ mean here?
qna.a: The human flesh that covers the body. viii) With solemn…… duty

qna.q: a) What are the various functions and objects given up by a defeated king?
qna.a: The deposed king throws away respect, form and ceremonious duty.

qna.q: b) Bring out King Richard’s feelings when he was defeated.
qna.a: Despair and a sense of resignation are the feelings of King Richard when he was defeated. FIGURES OF SPEECH
